prize_parts.citation: For their theory of how lobbying and special-interest politics shape trade policy, which turned protection from an exogenous wedge into an equilibrium outcome.

statement.case_for: My ballot and laureate names are unchanged. The Grossman-Helpman contribution is a compact equilibrium model in which tariffs result from lobbying and electoral incentives. It gave a whole policy area a structure that could be tested. Three decades of extension and empirical work on tariff structures and trade agreements show that the idea has been absorbed into the field. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a stable two-person partnership with jointly authored core papers. Round 1 changed the wording of my case, not the ballot. Strömberg is right that the citation should rest on the political-economy strand, where the overlap with the 2008 prize is weakest, and I have narrowed it accordingly. I now treat the mixed record of the specific Protection for Sale predictions as a real discount. I weigh it against the framework's role in organising later work, and on balance I still judge it sufficient for a prize. I do not count the support tallies as evidence of merit. The chair's summary shows that no configuration is near a majority and that first choices are dispersed, which is a fact about the room and says nothing about quality.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the empirical record. Tests of the specific functional form have been mixed, and Teorell calls the evidence thin. The estimated weights that governments place on welfare versus contributions have been debated, as far as I recall, and I have not verified this independently. The prize would reward a conceptual framework more than a settled empirical finding. Helpman is also credited on B041, so the two trade configurations compete for one laureate and the Committee must decide which achievement he is credited for. The 2008 trade prize may reduce appetite for a second trade award even though the strands differ. B038 offers more direct and measurable policy reach, and its attribution is now largely agreed on Autor, Hanson and Dorn. If the Committee gives empirical identification the main weight, B038 has the stronger claim.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved B013 from first choice to a close alternative. He cited the framing question of trade politics versus growth and trade, the overlap with B041 that complicates a Helpman award, and the mixed empirical record of the protection-for-sale predictions. He said B013 needs a narrower rationale than B038.
responses.response: I accept the narrower rationale and have written my citation that way: lobbying and special-interest politics as the determinant of trade policy, without a claim on the wider trade-theory programme. That also answers the framing worry. The Helpman overlap with B041 is a question for the Committee about which achievement to credit him for. It is not a reason to discount the Grossman-Helpman work, and I do not think a possible later recognition of Melitz should count against it. On the empirical point, I agree it is a real discount, but I would separate two things. Fredriksson's own identification-focused standard asks whether a framework has been taken to data and refined, and this one has been, even where the estimates are contested. I do not move to B038, because I still weigh conceptual depth and clean attribution at least as heavily as the stronger policy visibility of the labour evidence. B038 stays as my first alternative.

responses.point: Teorell did not rank B013. He finds the measurement and empirical support for the lobbying-contribution mechanism thin and wants more evidence of a transformative empirical effect before treating it as one. He acknowledges that its influence is not in doubt.
responses.response: I take this as the strongest objection to my first choice. I would answer in two parts. First, the framework's contribution is that it produced sharp, estimable predictions about which sectors are protected and how. That is why there is an empirical literature that can be mixed or contradictory at all. Earlier models of tariff politics did not allow this. Second, a prize can reward the idea and its consequences without requiring every prediction to survive. I do not claim a transformative empirical effect. I claim that the framework changed how trade policy is modelled and studied. If a member holds that empirical validation must be the main criterion, B038 and B002 are the better answers, and I would rank them above B013 on that criterion. I have not independently verified the empirical literature, and I do not think the supplied evidence resolves the dispute.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 (Melitz and Helpman) first. He argues for a single checkable discovery with a clear originator, over twenty years of confirmation, and a reorganisation of empirical trade work. He concedes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have parallel claims and that Helpman's credit is split between B041 and B013.
responses.response: I agree that B041 is a serious configuration and that Melitz is the originator of the core model. I would not oppose it on merit. My difference is attribution. By his own account the claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be honoured within the ballot, so the laureate set is contestable in a way the Grossman-Helpman pair is not. B041 is also the more direct successor to the new trade theory recognised in 2008, while B013 asks a different question, namely why policy takes the form it does. His fallback of Melitz alone is coherent, but it would separate the originator from the Helpman extension that he defends, and I find it less natural than either full configuration. Since the two compete for Helpman, I would ask the Committee to choose on the achievement and its attribution, and not to let one configuration displace the other by default.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B013 first, with a citation that also covers trade, innovation and growth in open economies. He argues that the Krugman overlap is weak for the political-economy and growth strands and that a Helpman award should not be blocked by a possible later Melitz recognition.
responses.response: I agree on the overlap argument and on not letting a hypothetical later Melitz award count against this one. I differ on citation scope. His wider wording adds the growth-and-trade strand, which strengthens the body of work but makes the citation depend on more than the shortlisted discovery. It would also draw the critique that the prize bundles two programmes, the same critique several of us make against B038. I therefore keep the citation to political economy and trade policy. If the Committee preferred a broader Grossman-Helpman citation, I would not object. I would want it justified by the growth-and-trade work on its own terms, and not used to make up for the mixed record on Protection for Sale.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first. He treats Rubinstein-Wolinsky as a deep, mature result with a clean split of credit, and he argues that its main risk is that recognition is overdue. He distinguishes it from earlier game-theory prizes.
responses.response: I ranked B001 seventh, so the disagreement is one of priority, not of validity. I accept that the alternating-offers model is canonical and that the credit between Rubinstein and Wolinsky is more settled than for most of the shortlist. I also accept his argument that it is a positive model of how negotiation unfolds and is therefore different from the earlier prizes on equilibrium refinement and mechanism design. Where I still differ is the empirical and policy content. B013 produced a literature that applies the model to tariff data and trade agreements. B001 mostly gave other fields a building block, which is real but harder to see in the evidence. That is a judgement about weighting and not a claim that B001 is the weaker work. If the Committee puts maturity and attribution first, B001 is a defensible outcome and I would not regard it as a mistake.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the mixed empirical record of the Protection for Sale predictions as a decisive discount or as secondary to the framework's influence.
Whether the 2008 trade prize leaves room for a second trade award, and whether Helpman should be credited for B013 or B041. A choice for one may foreclose the other.

Whether B038, with a citation limited to trade and technology exposure and local labour-market adjustment, has stronger scientific and policy reach than B013. Its Autor-Hanson-Dorn attribution has become much clearer, but the shift-share and persistence debates remain.
How much a prize in one area should be discounted for recent prizes on adjacent themes (2008, 2022, 2024), and whether the Committee applies one standard to all candidates.
My assessments rest on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, without independent verification of the empirical literature.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1. Giovanni Violante, a long-term co-author, is credited on B004. That framework builds on my own earlier heterogeneous-agent work with Anthony Smith, so I do not propose B004, name it as an alternative, or give it weight. I frequently co-author with John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member), and I am an IIES colleague of both. I have weighed their arguments on scientific merit, including Hassler's rival first choice B041. My own work on the political economy of growth and on the dynamics of government is thematically adjacent to B013 and B027. This is field proximity and not a connection to Grossman, Helpman, or the B038 and B012 candidates. As secretary I hold a procedural role, which gives me no additional claim on merit. No recusal is adjudicated here, and none of this is a claim about confidential proceedings.
